danish.title: Tredje bog (1805) — Kapitel 7
paragraphs: Den tolvte november forberedte Kutuzovs aktive hær, lejret foran Olmütz, sig på næste dags mønstring for de to kejsere — den russiske og den østrigske. Garden, der netop var ankommet fra Rusland, tilbragte natten femten kilometer fra Olmütz og skulle næste morgen marchere direkte til mønstringspladsen og nå feltet ved Olmütz klokken ti.

Den dag modtog Nikolaj Rostov et brev fra Boris, der fortalte ham, at Ismajlov-regimentet lå i kvarter femten kilometer fra Olmütz for natten, og at han gerne ville se ham, fordi han havde et brev og penge til ham. Rostov trængte i den grad til penge lige nu, hvor tropperne efter den aktive tjeneste var stationeret nær Olmütz, og lejren vrimlede med velforsynede marketendere og østrigske jøder, der tilbød alle slags fristende varer. Pavlograderne holdt det ene gilde efter det andet for at fejre de udmærkelser, de havde modtaget under felttoget, og de foretog udflugter til Olmütz for at besøge en vis Caroline fra Ungarn, der for nylig havde åbnet en restaurant med piger som tjenere. Rostov, der netop havde fejret sin forfremmelse til kornet og købt Denisovs hest Beduin, var forgældet til alle sider, både kammerater og marketendere. Da han modtog Boris' brev, red han med en kammerat til Olmütz, spiste middag der, drak en flaske vin og red så alene til gardelejren for at finde sin gamle legekammerat. Rostov havde endnu ikke fået sin nye uniform. Han bar en lurvet kadetjakke prydet med et soldaterkors, lige så lurvede kadet-ridebukser foret med slidt læder og en officerssabel med sabelkvast. Don-hesten, han red på, havde han købt af en kosak under felttoget, og han bar en krøllet husarhue skødesløst skubbet tilbage på den ene side af hovedet. Da han red op mod lejren, tænkte han på, hvordan han ville imponere Boris og alle hans kammerater i garden med sit udseende — som en kampvant husar, der havde været under ild.

Garden havde tilbagelagt hele marchen som en fornøjelsestur og paraderet med sin renlighed og disciplin. De var kommet i bekvemme etapper, deres tornyster kørt på vogne, og de østrigske myndigheder havde sørget for fremragende middage til officererne ved hvert rastested. Regimenterne havde rykket ind og ud af byerne med musikken spillende, og på storhertugens ordre havde soldaterne marcheret hele vejen i takt — en skik garden var stolt af — med officererne til fods på deres rette pladser. Boris havde været indkvarteret og marcheret hele vejen sammen med Berg, der allerede havde kommandoen over et kompagni. Berg, der havde opnået sin kaptajnsgrad under felttoget, havde vundet sine overordnedes tillid med sin punktlighed og nøjagtighed og havde ordnet sine pengesager yderst tilfredsstillende. Boris havde under felttoget gjort bekendtskab med mange personer, der kunne vise sig nyttige for ham, og gennem et anbefalingsbrev, han havde medbragt fra Pierre, var han blevet bekendt med fyrst Andrej Bolkonskij, gennem hvem han håbede at opnå en post ved overkommandoens stab. Berg og Boris, der havde hvilet efter gårsdagens march, sad rene og pænt klædte ved et rundt bord i de rene kvarterer, der var tildelt dem, og spillede skak. Berg holdt en rygende pibe mellem knæene. Boris, på den præcise måde der var karakteristisk for ham, var i færd med at bygge en lille pyramide af skakbrikker med sine slanke hvide fingre, mens han ventede på Bergs træk, og iagttog sin modstanders ansigt — han tænkte åbenbart over spillet, som han altid kun tænkte over det, han lige var i gang med.
»Nå, hvordan vil du komme ud af det?« bemærkede han.
»Det skal vi nok finde ud af,« svarede Berg, rørte ved en bonde og trak så hånden til sig.
I det øjeblik gik døren op.

»Der er han endelig!« råbte Rostov. »Og Berg med! Ih, I petisenfans, allé kusjé dormir!« udbrød han og efterlignede sin russiske barnepiges fransk, som han og Boris plejede at grine af for længe siden.
»Jøsses, hvor du har forandret dig!«

Boris rejste sig for at tage imod Rostov, men forsømte ikke dermed at holde fast i og stille nogle skakbrikker på plads, der var ved at falde. Han var ved at omfavne sin ven, men Nikolaj undveg ham. Med den særlige ungdommens følelse, den rædsel for slagne veje og ønsket om at udtrykke sig anderledes end de ældre — som ofte er uoprigtigt — ville Nikolaj gøre noget særligt, da han mødte sin ven. Han ville knibe ham, skubbe til ham, hvad som helst undtagen at kysse ham, som alle andre gjorde. Men uanset alt dette omfavnede Boris ham på sin stille, venlige måde og kyssede ham tre gange.

De havde ikke set hinanden i næsten et halvt år, og i den alder, hvor unge mænd tager deres første skridt på livets vej, så hver af dem umådelige forandringer i den anden — et helt nyt spejlbillede af det samfund, de havde taget de første skridt i. Begge var forandret meget, siden de sidst mødtes, og begge brændte efter at vise de forandringer, der var sket med dem.

»Åh, I forbandede lapsekyllingery! Rene og friske som om I havde været til fest, ikke som os syndere fra linjen!« råbte Rostov med militær bravur og med baritontoner i stemmen, der var nye for Boris, og pegede på sine egne mudderplettede bukser. Den tyske værtinde, der hørte Rostovs høje stemme, stak hovedet ind ad døren.
»Nå, er hun køn?« spurgte han med et blink.

»Hvorfor råber du sådan? Du skræmmer dem!« sagde Boris. »Jeg ventede dig ikke i dag,« tilføjede han. »Jeg sendte dig først beskeden i går med Bolkonskij — en adjudant hos Kutuzov, som er min ven. Jeg troede ikke, han ville få den frem til dig så hurtigt... Nå, hvordan har du det? Har du allerede været under ild?« spurgte Boris.
Uden at svare rystede Rostov Sankt Georgs-soldaterkorset, der var fæstet til uniformens snore, og med et blik på Berg viste han sin forbundne arm med et smil.
»Som du kan se,« sagde han.

»Virkelig? Ja, ja!« sagde Boris med et smil. »Og vi har også haft en glimrende march. I ved naturligvis, at Hans Kejserlige Højhed red med vores regiment hele tiden, så vi havde alle bekvemmeligheder og fordele. Sikke modtagelser vi fik i Polen! Sikke middage og baller! Jeg kan ikke beskrive det. Og tsarevitten var meget nådig mod alle vores officerer.«

Og de to venner fortalte hinanden om deres oplevelser — den ene om sine husareskapader og livet på frontlinjen, den anden om fornøjelserne og fordelene ved tjeneste under medlemmer af den kejserlige familie.
»Åh, I garder!« sagde Rostov. »Hør, send bud efter noget vin.«
Boris lavede en grimasse.
»Hvis du virkelig vil,« sagde han.
Han gik hen til sin seng, trak en pung frem under den rene pude og sendte bud efter vin.
»Ja, og jeg har også nogle penge og et brev at give dig,« tilføjede han.

Rostov tog brevet og smed pengene hen på sofaen, lagde begge arme på bordet og begyndte at læse. Efter at have læst nogle linjer kastede han et vredt blik på Berg, mødte så hans øjne og skjulte ansigtet bag brevet.
»Tja, de har sendt dig en pæn sum,« sagde Berg og betragtede den tunge pung, der sank ned i sofaen. »Hvad os angår, greve, klarer vi os på vores sold. Jeg kan sige for mig selv ...«

»Hør, Berg, min kære ven,« sagde Rostov, »når du får et brev hjemmefra og møder en af dine egne, som du vil snakke alting igennem med, og jeg tilfældigvis er til stede, så går jeg straks, for ikke at være i vejen! Gå et eller andet sted hen, hvor som helst ... til helvede!« udbrød han og greb ham straks i skulderen og så venligt ind i hans ansigt, åbenbart for at mildne grovheden i sine ord. »Bliv ikke fornærmet, min kære ven; du ved, jeg taler lige ud af hjertet som til en gammel bekendt.«
»Åh, det gør ikke noget, greve! Jeg forstår udmærket,« sagde Berg og rejste sig og talte med en dæmpet, gutturel stemme.
»Gå over til vores værtsfolk, de har inviteret dig,« tilføjede Boris.

Berg tog den reneste af sine frakker på, uden en plet eller et fnug, stillede sig foran et spejl og børstede håret ved tindingerne opad på den måde, kejser Alexander foretrak, og efter at have forvisset sig ud fra den måde, Rostov så på den, at hans frakke var blevet bemærket, forlod han værelset med et behageligt smil.
»Åh Gud, sikket et bæst jeg er!« mumlede Rostov, mens han læste brevet.
»Hvorffor?«

»Åh, sikken en gris jeg er, at jeg ikke har skrevet og har givet dem sådan en forskrækkelse! Åh, sikken en gris jeg er!« gentog han og blev pludselig rød i hovedet. »Nå, har du sendt Gabriel efter vin? Godt, lad os få noget!«

I brevet fra hans forældre lå et anbefalingsbrev til Bagration, som den gamle grevinde på Anna Mikhajlovnas (Boris' mor) råd havde skaffet gennem en bekendt og sendt til sin søn med anmodning om at aflevere det på sin adresse og gøre brug af det.
»Sikke noget pjat! Som om jeg har brug for det!« sagde Rostov og kastede brevet under bordet.
»Hvorfor smed du det væk?« spurgte Boris.
»Det er et eller andet anbefalingsbrev ... hvad pokker skal jeg bruge det til!«
»Hvorfor 'hvad pokker'?« sagde Boris, samlede det op og læste adressen. »Dette brev kan være til stor nytte for dig.«
»Jeg vil ingenting, og jeg vil ikke være nogens adjudant.«
»Hvorfor ikke?« spurgte Boris.
»Det er et lakajjob!«
»Du er stadig den samme drømmer, kan jeg se,« bemærkede Boris og rystede på hovedet.
»Og du er stadig den samme diplomat! Men det er ikke sagen... Nå, hvordan har du det?« spurgte Rostov.
»Tja, som du kan se. Hidtil er alt i orden, men jeg må tilstå, at jeg meget gerne ville være adjudant og ikke forblive ved fronten.«
»Hvorfor?«
»Fordi når man først har givet sig ind på militærtjeneste, bør man forsøge at gøre så god en karriere af det som muligt.«
»Nå, er det det!« sagde Rostov, tydeligvis optaget af noget andet.
Han så indtrængende og spørgende ind i sin vens øjne og prøvede åbenbart forgæves at finde svar på et eller andet spørgsmål.
Gamle Gabriel kom ind med vinen.
»Skulle vi ikke sende bud efter Berg?« spurgte Boris. »Han ville drikke med dig. Jeg kan ikke.«
»Ja, send bud efter ham ... og hvordan kommer du ud af det med den tysker?« spurgte Rostov med et foragteligt smil.
»Han er en meget, meget rar, ærlig og behagelig fyr,« svarede Boris.

Igen så Rostov indtrængende ind i Boris' øjne og sukkede. Berg vendte tilbage, og over vinflasken blev samtalen mellem de tre officerer livlig. Gardeofficererne fortalte Rostov om deres march, og hvordan de var blevet forkælet i Rusland, Polen og udlandet. De talte om storhertugens udtalelser og handlinger og fortalte historier om hans venlighed og hidsighed. Berg tav som sædvanlig, når emnet ikke vedrørte ham selv, men i forbindelse med historierne om storhertugens hidsige temperament fortalte han med velbehag om, hvordan han i Galicien havde klaret sig over for storhertugen, da denne havde foretaget en inspektion af regimenterne og blev vred over en uregelmæssighed i en bevægelse. Med et behageligt smil fortalte Berg, hvordan storhertugen var redet op til ham i voldsomt raseri og havde råbt: »Arnaouter!« ('Arnaouter' var tsarevittens yndlingsudtryk, når han var ophidset) og kaldt på kompagnichefen.

»Vil I tro det, greve, jeg var slet ikke bange, for jeg vidste, at jeg havde ret. Uden at prale, ved I, kan jeg sige, at jeg kender arméens befalinger udenad og kender reglementet lige så godt som Fadervor. Så, greve, der er aldrig forsømmelighed i mit kompagni, og min samvittighed var derfor ren. Jeg trådte frem ...« (Berg rejste sig og viste, hvordan han havde præsenteret sig med hånden ved huen, og det ville virkelig have været svært for et ansigt at udtrykke større respekt og selvtilfredshed end hans.) »Nå, han tordnede løs mod mig, som man siger, tordnede og tordnede og tordnede! Det var ikke et spørgsmål om liv, men snarere om død, som man siger. 'Albanere!' og 'djævle!' og 'Til Sibirien!' sagde Berg med et klogt smil. »Jeg vidste, at jeg havde ret, så jeg tav stille — var det ikke bedst, greve? ... 'Hør, er du stum?' råbte han. Alligevel tav jeg. Og hvad tror I, greve? Næste dag blev det ikke engang nævnt i dagens befalinger. Det er, hvad det vil sige at bevare fatningen. Sådan skal det gøres, greve,« sagde Berg og tændte sin pibe og pustede røgringe ud.
»Ja, det var flot,« sagde Rostov med et smil.

Men Boris bemærkede, at han var ved at gøre sig klar til at drive gæk med Berg, og førte behændigt samtalen hen på et andet emne. Han bad ham fortælle, hvordan og hvor han var blevet såret. Det behagede Rostov, og han begyndte at fortælle og blev mere og mere ivrig, som han fortsatte. Han fortalte dem om sit Schön Grabern-eventyr, præcis som dem, der har deltaget i en kamp, gerne beskriver den — det vil sige, som de gerne ville have, at det var foregået, som de har hørt det beskrevet af andre, og som det lyder godt, men slet ikke som det virkelig var. Rostov var en sandfærdig ung mand og ville under ingen omstændigheder have fortalt en bevidst løgn. Han begyndte sin historie med den hensigt at fortælle alt, præcis som det var sket, men umærkeligt, ufrivilligt og uundgåeligt gled han ind i usandhed. Hvis han havde fortalt sandheden til sine tilhørere — der ligesom han selv ofte havde hørt historier om angreb og havde dannet sig en klar forestilling om, hvad et angreb var, og forventede at høre netop sådan en historie — ville de enten ikke have troet ham eller, endnu værre, have ment, at Rostov selv var skyld i det, siden det, der normalt sker for dem, der fortæller om kavalerichok, ikke var sket for ham. Han kunne ikke bare fortælle dem, at alle red af sted i trav, og at han faldt af hesten, forstuvede sin arm og så løb alt hvad han kunne væk fra en franskmand ind i skoven. Desuden ville det for at fortælle alt, som det virkelig var, have krævet en viljesanstrengelse kun at fortælle, hvad der virkelig skete. Det er meget svært at fortælle sandheden, og unge mennesker er sjældent i stand til det. Hans tilhørere ventede en historie om, hvordan han var ude af sig selv og brændende af begejstring, havde styrtet som en storm mod karréen, hugget sig igennem, hugget til højre og venstre, hvordan hans sabel havde smagt kød, og han var faldet om udmattet, og så videre. Og det var, hvad han fortalte dem.

Midt i sin fortælling, netop som han sagde: »I kan ikke forestille jer, hvilket mærkeligt vanvid man oplever under et angreb,« trådte fyrst Andrej (Bolkonskij), som Boris ventede, ind i værelset. Fyrst Andrej, der gerne hjalp unge mænd, var smigret over at blive bedt om sin bistand, og da han var velvilligt stemt over for Boris, der havde formået at gøre et godt indtryk på ham dagen før, ønskede han at gøre det, den unge mand bad om. Da han havde været sendt med papirer fra Kutuzov til tsarevitten, kiggede han ind til Boris i håb om at finde ham alene. Da han kom ind og så en linjehusar genfortælle sine militære bedrifter — fyrst Andrej kunne ikke udstå den slags mennesker — gav han Boris et venligt smil, rynkede brynene, mens han med halvlukkede øjne så på Rostov, nikkede let og træt og satte sig slapt i sofaen; det var ham ubehageligt at være dumpet ind i dårligt selskab. Rostov rødmede, da han bemærkede det, men det var ham ligegyldigt — det var jo bare en fremmed. Da han imidlertid kastede et blik på Boris, så han, at denne også syntes at skamme sig over linjehusaren.

Trods fyrst Andrejs ubehagelige, ironiske tone, trods den foragt hvormed Rostov fra sit frontsynspunkt betragtede alle disse små stabsadjudanter, som den nyankomne åbenbart var en af, følte Rostov sig forvirret, rødmede og blev tavs. Boris spurgte, hvilke nyheder der måtte være fra staben, og hvad man uden indiskretion kunne spørge om angående vores planer.
»Vi rykker sandsynligvis frem,« svarede Bolkonskij, tydeligt uvillig til at sige mere i en fremmeds nærværelse.

Berg benyttede lejligheden til med stor høflighed at spørge, om det, som rygtet sagde, var sandt, at foderafløsningen til kompagnichefer ville blive fordoblet. Hertil svarede fyrst Andrej med et smil, at han ikke kunne udtale sig om en så vigtig regeringsbeslutning, og Berg lo muntert.
»Hvad angår din sag,« fortsatte fyrst Andrej henvendt til Boris, »taler vi om det senere.« Han så sig om mod Rostov. »Kom til mig efter mønstringen, så gør vi, hvad der kan gøres.«

Og efter at have set sig om i værelset vendte fyrst Andrej sig mod Rostov, hvis tilstand af uovervindelig barnlig forlegenhed, der nu skiftede til vrede, han ikke nedlod sig til at bemærke, og sagde: »Jeg tror, De talte om Schön Grabern-affæren? Var De der?«
»Jeg var der,« sagde Rostov vredt, som om han agtede at fornærme adjudanten.
Bolkonskij bemærkede husarens sindstilstand, og det morede ham. Med et let foragteligt smil sagde han: »Ja, der fortælles mange historier om den affære nu!«

»Ja, historier!« gentog Rostov højt og så med øjne, der pludselig var blevet rasende, snart på Boris, snart på Bolkonskij. »Ja, mange historier! Men vores historier er historier fra mænd, der har været under fjendens ild! Vores historier har nogen vægt, ikke som historierne fra de stabsfyre, der får belønninger uden at bestille noget!«
»Hvem De forestiller Dem, jeg er en af?« sagde fyrst Andrej med et stille og særlig elskværdigt smil.
En mærkelig følelse af ophidselse og dog respekt for denne mands selvbeherskelse blandede sig i det øjeblik i Rostovs sjæl.
»Jeg taler ikke om Dem,« sagde han, »jeg kender Dem ikke og vil helt ærligt ikke kende Dem. Jeg taler om staben generelt.«

»Og jeg vil sige Dem dette,« afbrød fyrst Andrej med stille autoritet i stemmen. »De ønsker at fornærme mig, og jeg er rede til at give Dem ret i, at det ville være meget let, hvis De ikke har tilstrækkelig selvrespekt; men indrøm, at tiden og stedet er meget dårligt valgt. Om en dag eller to skal vi alle deltage i en større og mere alvorlig duel, og desuden er Drubetskoj, der siger han er Deres gamle ven, slet ikke skyld i, at mit ansigt har den ulykke at mishage Dem. Men,« tilføjede han og rejste sig, »De kender mit navn og ved, hvor De kan finde mig; men glem ikke, at jeg hverken betragter mig selv eller Dem som fornærmet, og mit råd som den ældre er at lade sagen falde. Nå altså, på fredag efter mønstringen venter jeg Dem, Drubetskoj. Farvel!« udbrød fyrst Andrej og forlod dem begge med en hilsen.

Først da fyrst Andrej var gået, kom Rostov i tanke om, hvad han burde have sagt. Og han var endnu mere vred over at have forsømt at sige det. Han beordrede straks sin hest og tog køligt afsked med Boris og red hjem. Skulle han ride til hovedkvarteret næste dag og udfordre den affekterede adjudant, eller virkelig lade sagen falde — det var det spørgsmål, der plagede ham hele vejen. Han tænkte vredt på den fornøjelse, det ville være at se den frygtsomme mine hos den lille, spinkle, men stolte mand, når han blev dækket af hans pistol, og så følte han med overraskelse, at af alle de mennesker han kendte, var der ingen, han så gerne ville have til ven, som netop den adjudant, han hadede så meget.

english.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: On the twelfth of November, Kutuzov's army was camped outside Olmutz, preparing for a review the next day by both Emperors — Russian and Austrian. The Guards, having just arrived from Russia, spent the night ten miles away and were to march straight to the review field at Olmutz by ten the next morning.

That day, Nicholas Rostov received a letter from Boris saying that the Ismaylov regiment was camped ten miles from Olmutz for the night, and that Boris wanted to see him because he had a letter and money for him. Rostov badly needed money just then. Now that the troops were stationed near Olmutz after their active campaigning, the camp was swarming with well-stocked merchants and Austrian Jews selling all kinds of tempting goods. The Pavlograds threw one celebration after another to mark the awards they'd earned during the campaign, and made regular trips to Olmutz to visit a certain Caroline the Hungarian, who had recently opened a restaurant there with girls as waitresses. Rostov, who had just celebrated his promotion to cornet and bought Denisov's horse Bedouin, was in debt to everyone — his comrades and the merchants alike. When he got Boris's letter, he rode to Olmutz with a fellow officer, had dinner, drank a bottle of wine, and then set off alone to the Guards' camp to find his childhood friend. He hadn't had time to get a proper uniform yet. He wore a shabby cadet jacket with a soldier's cross pinned to it, equally worn cadet riding breeches with leather patches, and an officer's saber with a sword knot. The Don horse he rode was one he'd bought from a Cossack during the campaign, and he wore a crumpled hussar cap pushed jauntily to one side. As he rode toward the camp, he imagined the impression he would make on Boris and his Guards comrades — that of a battle-hardened hussar who had actually been under fire.

The Guards had marched the whole way as if on a pleasure trip, showing off their cleanliness and discipline. They'd traveled in easy stages, their packs carried on carts, and the Austrian authorities had provided excellent dinners for the officers at every stop. The regiments had entered and left each town with bands playing, and by the Grand Duke's orders, the men had marched in perfect step the entire way — a point of pride for the Guards — with officers on foot at their proper posts. Boris had been quartered and had marched all the way with Berg, who now commanded a company. Berg had earned his captaincy during the campaign and had won his superiors' trust through his punctuality and precision. He'd also managed his finances very satisfactorily. During the campaign, Boris had made the acquaintance of several useful people and, armed with a letter of introduction from Pierre, had gotten to know Prince Andrew Bolkonsky, through whom he hoped to land a position on the commander-in-chief's staff. Berg and Boris, rested after yesterday's march, were sitting clean and neatly dressed at a round table in their tidy quarters, playing chess. Berg held a lit pipe between his knees. Boris, with his characteristic precision, was building a little pyramid of chess pieces with his slender white fingers while waiting for Berg's move, his mind clearly focused entirely on the game — as was always the case with whatever he happened to be doing.
"Well, how are you going to get out of that?" he said.
"I'll figure something out," Berg replied, touching a pawn and then pulling his hand back.
At that moment the door opened.

"Here he is at last!" Rostov shouted. "And Berg too! Oh, you little kids, go to sleep!" he exclaimed, mangling the French phrase the way his Russian nanny used to, which he and Boris had always found hilarious.
"My goodness, how you've changed!"

Boris stood up to greet Rostov, but carefully steadied some chess pieces that were about to topple over. He moved to embrace his friend, but Nicholas dodged him. With that instinct of youth — the fear of well-worn paths, the desire to express itself differently from older people who are often insincere — Nicholas wanted to do something distinctive when greeting his friend. He wanted to poke him, shove him, anything but kiss him, which was what everyone did. But Boris embraced him anyway, calmly and warmly, and kissed him three times.

They hadn't seen each other for nearly half a year, and at the age when young men are taking their first steps in life, each saw enormous changes in the other — a whole new reflection of the world they'd each entered. Both had changed drastically since their last meeting, and both were eager to show off the transformations.

"Oh, you pampered dandies! Clean and polished like you're going to a ball — not like us poor infantry sinners," Rostov cried with military swagger, his voice now carrying new baritone notes that were unfamiliar to Boris, as he pointed at his own mud-splattered breeches. The German landlady, hearing Rostov's booming voice, stuck her head through the door.
"Hey — is she pretty?" he asked with a wink.

"Why are you yelling like that? You'll scare them!" Boris said. "I wasn't expecting you today. I only sent the note yesterday through Bolkonsky — one of Kutuzov's adjutants, a friend of mine. I didn't think he'd deliver it so fast... So, how are you? Have you been under fire yet?" Boris asked.
Instead of answering, Rostov shook the soldier's Cross of St. George pinned to his jacket, indicated his bandaged arm, and looked at Berg with a smile.
"See for yourself," he said.

"Really? Well, well!" said Boris, smiling. "We've had quite a fine march ourselves, you know. His Imperial Highness rode with our regiment the entire time, so we had every comfort and advantage. The receptions we got in Poland! The dinners and balls! You wouldn't believe it. And the Tsarevich was very gracious to all the officers."
And so the two friends traded stories — one about his hussar adventures and life on the front lines, the other about the pleasures and perks of serving under members of the Imperial family.
"Oh, you Guards!" said Rostov. "Hey, send for some wine."
Boris made a face.
"If you really want it," he said.
He went to his bed, pulled a purse from under the spotless pillow, and sent for wine.
"Yes, and I have some money and a letter to give you," he added.

Rostov took the letter and, tossing the money onto the sofa, propped both arms on the table and began to read. After a few lines, he glanced angrily at Berg, then, catching his eye, hid his face behind the letter.
"Well, they've sent you a nice sum," said Berg, eyeing the heavy purse sinking into the sofa cushions. "As for us, Count, we get along on our pay. Speaking for myself..."

"Listen, Berg, my dear fellow," Rostov said, "when you get a letter from home and run into someone you've known all your life and want to pour your heart out to — and I happen to be there — I'll leave immediately so I'm not in the way. Please go somewhere, anywhere... go to hell!" he burst out, then immediately grabbed Berg by the shoulder and, looking kindly into his face to soften the harshness, added: "Don't take offense, old friend. I'm speaking from the heart, as one old acquaintance to another."
"Oh, not at all, Count! I completely understand," said Berg, getting up and speaking in his muffled, throaty voice.
"Go visit our hosts — they invited you," Boris added.

Berg put on his cleanest coat — without a single spot or speck of dust — stood before a mirror and brushed his temple hair upward in the style made fashionable by Emperor Alexander. Having satisfied himself from Rostov's glance that his coat had been noticed, he left the room with a pleased smile.
"Oh God, what a beast I am!" Rostov muttered as he read the letter.
"Why?"

"What a horrible person I am — not writing to them and giving them such a scare! What a horrible person!" he repeated, suddenly flushing. "Well, has Gabriel gone for the wine? Good — let's have some!"

Enclosed with his parents' letter was a letter of recommendation to Bagration, which the old countess had obtained through a connection at Anna Mikhaylovna's suggestion and sent along for Nicholas to deliver and make use of.
"What nonsense! As if I need this!" said Rostov, tossing the letter under the table.
"Why did you throw that away?" Boris asked.
"It's some letter of recommendation... what the hell do I need it for!"
"What do you mean, 'what the hell'?" said Boris, picking it up and reading the address. "This letter could be extremely useful to you."
"I don't need anything, and I refuse to be anyone's errand boy."
"Why not?" Boris asked.
"It's a lackey's job!"
"You're still the same dreamer, I see," Boris remarked, shaking his head.
"And you're still the same diplomat! But that's beside the point... Come on, how are things with you?" Rostov asked.
"Well, as you can see, everything's fine so far. But I'll admit I'd really like to become an adjutant rather than stay at the front."
"Why?"
"Because once a man enters military service, he should try to make the most successful career of it that he can."
"Ah, is that so?" Rostov said, clearly thinking about something else.
He stared intently and searchingly into his friend's eyes, as though trying in vain to find the answer to some question.
Old Gabriel brought in the wine.
"Should we send for Berg?" Boris asked. "He'll drink with you. I can't."
"Sure, send for him... So how do you get along with that German?" Rostov asked with a dismissive smile.
"He's a very, very nice, honest, and pleasant fellow," Boris replied.

Again Rostov studied Boris's eyes intently, then sighed. Berg came back, and the three officers' conversation grew lively over the bottle of wine. The Guardsmen told Rostov about their march and how warmly they'd been received in Russia, Poland, and abroad. They talked about the Grand Duke — his sayings and habits — and shared stories of his kindness and his terrible temper. Berg, as usual, stayed quiet whenever the subject didn't concern him, but when it came to stories about the Grand Duke's outbursts, he eagerly described how, during an inspection in Galicia, he had handled the Grand Duke's fury. With a self-satisfied smile, Berg recounted how the Grand Duke had ridden up to him in a rage, shouting "Arnauts!" — the Tsarevich's favorite word when he was furious — and demanded to see the company commander.

"Would you believe it, Count — I wasn't the least bit nervous, because I knew I was in the right. Without meaning to boast, I can say that I know the Army Orders by heart and know the Regulations as well as I know the Lord's Prayer. So there's never any sloppiness in my company, and my conscience was clear. I stepped forward..." Berg stood up to demonstrate how he'd presented himself, hand at his cap, and it would have been hard to find a face expressing greater respect and self-satisfaction. "Well, he stormed at me — stormed and stormed and stormed! It wasn't about life so much as death, as the saying goes. 'Albanians!' and 'devils!' and 'off to Siberia!'" Berg said with a knowing smile. "I knew I was right, so I kept quiet. Wasn't that the best approach, Count? 'Hey, can’t you speak?' he yelled. I still said nothing. And guess what, Count? The next day there wasn't a word about it in the daily orders. That's what keeping your head gets you. That's how it's done, Count," Berg concluded, lighting his pipe and blowing smoke rings.
"Yes, that was well done," said Rostov with a smile.

But Boris noticed Rostov was gearing up to make fun of Berg and skillfully changed the subject. He asked Rostov to tell them how and where he'd been wounded. This pleased Rostov, and he launched into the story, growing more animated as he went. He described the action at Schon Grabern the way people who've been in battle usually do — not as it actually happened, but as they wished it had, as they'd heard others describe it, as it sounded good. Rostov was an honest young man who would never tell a deliberate lie. He started out intending to describe everything exactly as it occurred, but gradually, involuntarily, inevitably, he slid into invention. If he'd told his listeners the plain truth — listeners who, like him, had heard plenty of battle stories and had a fixed idea of what a cavalry charge should sound like — they either wouldn't have believed him or, worse, would have thought Rostov himself was to blame for things not going the way such stories usually went. He couldn't just say that everyone rode forward at a trot, that he fell off his horse and sprained his arm, and then ran as fast as he could into the woods to escape a Frenchman. Besides, telling the unvarnished truth would have required a deliberate effort of will to describe only what had actually happened. Telling the truth is very hard, and young people are rarely capable of it. His listeners expected to hear how he'd been beside himself with excitement, how he'd charged the enemy like a whirlwind, cut his way through, slashing left and right, how his saber had tasted blood and he'd fallen from exhaustion. And that's what he told them.

In the middle of his story — just as he was saying, "You can't imagine what a strange frenzy comes over you during a charge" — Prince Andrew walked in. Boris had been expecting him. Prince Andrew, who enjoyed helping young men and was flattered to be asked for assistance, was well-disposed toward Boris, who had impressed him the day before, and wanted to help. Having been sent with documents from Kutuzov to the Tsarevich, he'd stopped by to see Boris, hoping to find him alone. When he entered and saw a front-line hussar holding forth about his military exploits — the type of person Prince Andrew couldn't stand — he gave Boris a friendly smile but frowned, half-closing his eyes as he looked at Rostov. He gave a slight, weary bow and sat down on the sofa with an air of languid boredom, clearly regretting that he'd walked in on such company. Rostov flushed when he noticed this, but he didn't care — this was just some stranger. Glancing at Boris, however, he could see that Boris, too, seemed embarrassed by the front-line hussar.

Despite Prince Andrew's unpleasant, mocking tone, and despite the contempt Rostov felt — from his fighting soldier's perspective — for all these little staff adjutants (which the newcomer clearly was), Rostov felt flustered. He blushed and fell silent. Boris asked what news there was from headquarters and what, without being indiscreet, one might learn about their plans.
"We'll probably advance," Bolkonsky replied, evidently reluctant to say more with a stranger present.

Berg seized the opportunity to ask, with elaborate politeness, whether it was true that the forage allowance for company captains would be doubled. Prince Andrew answered with a smile that he couldn't offer an opinion on such an important government matter, and Berg laughed delightedly.
"As for your business," Prince Andrew continued, turning to Boris, "we'll discuss it later." He glanced around at Rostov. "Come see me after the review and we'll see what can be arranged."

Then, looking around the room, Prince Andrew turned to Rostov — whose state of obvious, childish embarrassment, now giving way to anger, he didn't deign to acknowledge — and said: "I believe you were talking about the action at Schon Grabern? Were you there?"
"I was there," Rostov said aggressively, as if meaning to insult the adjutant.
Bolkonsky noticed the hussar's hostile mood, and it amused him. With a slightly condescending smile, he said: "Yes, quite a few stories are circulating about that engagement."

"Yes, stories!" Rostov repeated loudly, his eyes blazing with sudden fury as he looked from Boris to Bolkonsky. "Yes, plenty of stories! But our stories come from men who've actually been under enemy fire! Our stories carry some weight — not like the tales of staff officers who collect medals without doing a thing!"
"Is that what you think I am?" Prince Andrew asked with a calm, notably pleasant smile.
A strange mixture of rage and reluctant respect for this man's composure churned in Rostov at that moment.
"I'm not talking about you," he said. "I don't know you and, frankly, I don't want to. I'm talking about the staff in general."

"Then let me say this," Prince Andrew interrupted, his voice quiet but carrying unmistakable authority. "You clearly want to insult me, and I'll grant you it would be easy enough if you lack basic self-respect. But I'd suggest the time and place are poorly chosen. In a day or two we'll all be engaged in a far greater and more serious contest. Besides, Drubetskoy here — who says he's an old friend of yours — is hardly to blame because you find my face disagreeable. In any case," he added, rising, "you know my name and where to find me. But I want you to understand that I consider neither myself nor you insulted. And as someone older than you, my advice would be to let the whole thing drop. So then — Friday after the review, Drubetskoy, I'll be expecting you. Goodbye!" Prince Andrew bowed to them both and left.

Only after Prince Andrew was gone did Rostov think of what he should have said. And he was even angrier at himself for having failed to say it. He immediately called for his horse and, taking a cold leave of Boris, rode home. Should he ride to headquarters the next day and challenge that arrogant adjutant, or should he just let it go? This question tormented him the entire way. He thought furiously about the pleasure of seeing that small, slight, proud man's fear when facing his pistol — and then felt a surge of surprise, because of all the people he knew, there was no one he'd rather have as a friend than that very adjutant he hated so much.
